item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a gravity-powered mountain trike designed to extend mountain tourism beyond the ski season is among the projects from the University of Ljubljana.

Also featured is biodegradable play equipment made from urban leaf waste and a multisensory exhibition system designed to make artworks more accessible to blind and partially sighted visitors.

University of Ljubljana

Institution: University of Ljubljana
School: Academy of Fine Arts and Design
Course: Industrial Design (BA), Industrial Design (MA), Graphic Design (BA)
Tutors: Patrik Bevec, Boštjan Botas Kenda, Žan Brezec, Rok Kuhar, Tamara Lašič Jurković, Jure Miklavc, Barbara Predan, Tim Prezelj and Barbara Prinčič

School statement:

"At the University of Ljubljana's Academy of Fine Arts and Design, industrial design is taught as a critical, research-led practice for engaging with the social, technological and environmental conditions shaping contemporary life.

"Slovenia's only university-level industrial design programme offers a continuous path from BA and MA study into interdisciplinary doctoral research, bringing together design practice, theory, strategic thinking and material experimentation.

"Project-based teaching sits at the centre of the programme. Students work across disciplines and within an internationally connected network of academic, public and private partners, addressing real-world challenges through product and service design, circular strategies, social innovation and critical speculation.

"They develop ideas through research, prototyping and testing, supported by tutors whose expertise spans academic inquiry and professional practice.

"The programme is further distinguished by its research in design culture and visual literacy. This foundation enables students to question established assumptions, understand how design shapes behaviour and meaning, and communicate complex ideas with clarity.

"It also expands the field beyond conventional human-centred approaches to consider systems, environments and more-than-human perspectives.

"The projects presented here show this approach in action: from biodegradable materials and inclusive exhibition tools to shared mobility, speculative interfaces and new models for year-round tourism.

"Together, they demonstrate how rigorous research, experimental thinking and close engagement with context can produce design that is imaginative, responsible and relevant."

Leafo by Iva Ferlinc and Maja Selinšek

"Leafo transforms urban leaf waste into biodegradable tools for open-ended sand play.

"Developed as an alternative to plastic beach and playground toys, the project connects two overlooked urban conditions: the disappearance of sandpits from public playgrounds and the seasonal accumulation of fallen leaves, often burned as waste.

"Processed leaves are combined with natural binders and plant-based pigments to create tactile, nature-inspired forms that invite sensory exploration, imagination and experimentation.

"After use, the tools can be composted, returning to the soil to complete a regenerative material cycle."

Students: Iva Ferlinc and Maja Selinšek
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Tamara Lašič Jurković, Jure Miklavc, Barbara Predan, Tim Prezelj and Barbara Prinčič
Email: iva.ferlinc[at]outlook.com and maja.selinsek[at]gmail.com

Hella Atmospheric Lighting by Žan Brezec and Rok Kuhar

"Developed in collaboration with international automotive lighting specialist Hella, this project reimagines the parked car as a portable social hub.

"Extending atmospheric lighting beyond the vehicle interior, it combines a car-body lighting system with a responsive digital service.

"The physical system projects light into the surrounding environment, while the service generates visual scenarios based on location, mood and user preferences.

"Together, they allow drivers and passengers to transform campsites, viewpoints and other temporary gathering places into immersive, personalised settings.

"By treating the car as more than transport, the project explores how automotive lighting can shape shared experiences beyond the road."

Students: Žan Brezec and Rok Kuhar
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Žan Brezec, Rok Kuhar and Jure Miklavc

Multisensory Exhibition Experience by Zoja Čepin

"This multisensory exhibition system makes artworks accessible beyond sight by combining layered tactile booklets with audio description.

"Each booklet translates an artwork into three progressively detailed tactile layers, allowing visitors to move from composition to key features at their own pace.

"Developed through interviews and testing with blind and partially sighted people, the system is simple to produce, affordable and easy to integrate into displays without altering them.

"Museums and galleries can adapt it with communities for permanent or temporary exhibitions, while visitors may take the booklets home.

"The result is a richer, more inclusive encounter with art for everyone."

Student: Zoja Čepin
Course: Industrial Design (BA)
Tutor: Jure Miklavc
Email: zoja.cepin[at]gmail.com

Šerkul – a circular bike-sharing service for Ljubljana by Patrik Bevec

"Šerkul is a station-free bicycle-sharing service that turns Ljubljana's discarded bikes into a shared urban resource.

"Recovered bicycles are repaired in a community workshop – fitted with GPS trackers and 3D-printed locks – and added to a mobile platform where users can locate and select them by size.

"Rather than building docking infrastructure, the service operates through a network of cultural institutions, public organisations, cafes and shops.

"Cycling earns users "green points", redeemable for benefits such as library membership or partner services.

"By connecting repair, reuse, shared mobility and local rewards, Šerkul creates a circular system that keeps bicycles and value moving."

Student: Patrik Bevec
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutor: Patrik Bevec

Sustainable Goat-Cheese Packaging for Kumparička Organic Farm by Lina Glavan, Ana Kovačič, Špela Novak and Vita Puc

"This concept for Kumparička Organic Farm in Istria turns goat's cheese into a sensory encounter with its origin.

"The pack pairs the cheese with herbs inspired by the Istrian landscape and a recipe for marinated goat's cheese, extending the experience beyond the product itself.

"A foldable structure brings together paper partly made from olive waste, biodegradable whey-based bioplastic, untreated jute and recycled cardboard.

"Rooted in the farm's visual identity, its Mediterranean character connects packaging with landscape, craft and food culture while reducing reliance on conventional packaging materials."

Students: Lina Glavan, Ana Kovačič, Špela Novak and Vita Puc
Course: Industrial Design (BA) and Graphic Design (BA)
Tutors: Boštjan Botas Kenda and Rok Kuhar
Email: lina.glavan[at]gmail.com, spela.novak01[at]gmail.com, pucvita[at]gmail.com and ana003.kovi[at]gmail.com

Carrot Reader by Pia Golob, Florian Janez Gutmann, Maja Selinšek and Jovana Mališić

"Developed within the subject History and Theory of Critical Design, Carrot Reader challenges anthropocentric design by casting a houseplant as a tarot reader.

"Instead of allowing users to choose the cards, the device uses data from a moisture sensor in the plant to generate a different combination for every question.

"Giving a non-human participant control over the outcome, the project reverses hierarchies between people, technology and nature.

"Designed as a speculative companion for the home or office, Carrot Reader proposes an unusual exchange: the plant receives water and care, while its human caretaker receives more-than-human guidance in return."

Students: Pia Golob, Florian Janez Gutmann, Maja Selinšek and Jovana Mališić
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Tamara Lašič Jurković and Barbara Predan
Email: piagolob01[at]gmail.com, gutmann.florian[at]gmail.com, maja.selinsek[at]gmail.com and jovanamalishic[at]gmail.com

Antidote – a gravity-powered mountain trike by Matic Čič and Vid Lebič

"Antidote is a gravity-powered mountain trike steered with the whole body through an innovative pendulum-based mechanism.

"By translating the rider's weight shifts into smooth, carving-like turns, it creates a downhill experience between sledding, skiing and mountain biking.

"Developed with input from ski-resort operators and refined through iterative testing, the project culminated in a fully functional prototype.

"Responding to snow-scarce winters, it enables lower-altitude resorts to extend their offering beyond the ski season by reusing existing slopes and lift infrastructure.

"With no onboard motor and minimal need for new construction, Antidote proposes a low-impact route towards year-round mountain tourism."

Students: Matic Čič and Vid Lebič
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Jure Miklavc and Barbara Predan
Email: Matic[at]cic.si and ebic.vid[at]gmail.com

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Pearce+ has added a wildlife tower for bats, owls, kestrels, invertebrates and wetland species at Honeygar Farm in Somerset, UK.

Built almost entirely from reclaimed materials found on the farm, the wildlife tower forms part of a wider plan to restore a wetland habitat on the Somerset Levels.

"The core idea was to create a long-term piece of wildlife infrastructure that could stand the test of time and provide opportunities for as many different species as possible," Pearce+ founding director Owen Pearce told Dezeen.

"It sits within the wider wetland restoration of Honeygar, where Somerset Wildlife Trust is transforming a former farm into restored wetland habitat alongside a new research and education centre."

The tower was designed to become a home for numerous species of animals, which determined its overall form.

"Rather than designing a house for one species, we've tried to create the conditions for lots of different wildlife to move in," said Pearce.

Read:

Invisible Studio & Pearce+ top domed woodworking pavilion with aluminium shingles

"Different species need to nest or roost at particular heights, so the overall height of the tower is partly dictated by the animals it is designed for," he continued.

"Barn owls, for example, naturally seek elevated, protected nesting places. The size of the upper structure is then determined by the dimensions of the different wildlife boxes housed inside it."

The tower was built on masonry piers made from reclaimed materials as the site regularly floods. Above this, the structure was made from reclaimed timber and corrugated metal.

"The idea of the site's restoration informed how we built the tower," said Pearce.

"We wanted to use as few new materials as possible, instead reclaiming materials that were already available on the farm and giving them a new purpose as habitat."

According to Pearce, the process of utilising reclaimed materials added a challenge to the construction process.

"The biggest challenge is the amount of work and uncertainty involved," he said. "Reuse sounds simple but you have to find the materials, dig them out, move them, clean them, assess them and then work out how they can actually be incorporated into the building."

"You can design with an idea of what materials are available, but until you start building there is always an element of the unknown," he continued.

Along with specific spaces for barn owls, kestrels and bats, Pearce hopes that the structure will also become home to a wider variety of wildlife.

"The tower is intended to work at lots of different scales," said Pearce. "Untreated timber can provide habitat for moths, spiders, woodlice and other invertebrates."

"The reclaimed masonry has cracks, textures and cavities that insects and small animals can inhabit, while openings within the piers could be used by amphibians or small mammals. Rubble and earth around the base creates a hibernaculum, a damp habitat that might suit newts, slow worms and other wetland species," he continued.

"We've provided the infrastructure, but ultimately wildlife will decide how to occupy it. In a way, the exciting part is that the building isn't finished when we leave – its inhabitants will complete it."

Previously, Pearce+ created a temporary sub-zero restaurant in Canada and a woodworking shelter at Westonbirt arboretum in Gloucestershire.

The photography is by Samuel Bray.

item.content:encoded:
Designers from IKEA and Xbox were paired up to create the products in this furniture collection, including a stool that looks and tilts like a giant thumbstick.

Unveiled today at the Gamescom fair in Cologne, the nine-piece YXSTABY range is Xbox's debut foray into gaming furniture, designed to blend easily into the home when it's out of action.

"We set out to make furniture people really want in their home, not furniture they accept because it is what you need to game," said IKEA product design developer Philip Dilé.

Each of the pieces in the collection was designed by a team made up of one IKEA designer and one Xbox designer, uniting their gaming and furniture design expertise.

The standout product is a stool modelled on the distinctive thumbsticks found on Xbox controllers.

"We were looking at which objects people actually have around them when they play, and the thumbstick kept looking like a small stool to us," IKEA designer David Wahl told Dezeen.

Adapted from original 3D models of the device, the stool features a curved base that allows it to tilt in all directions much like the real thumbstick, allowing users to lean into the action.

The seat even has the same grippy tessellated edges, now serving to hold the sitter rather than their thumbs in place.

"The challenge wasn't creating a giant thumbstick; the challenge was creating a great stool that still felt like a thumbstick," Xbox design director Elliot Hsu explained.

"We went back to the controller's original design files and spent a lot of time refining the proportions, texture, seating curve and stability. We wanted people to recognize it instantly while still feeling comfortable and functional in a living room."

Other pieces that play on some of Xbox's recognisable design elements include a shiny stainless-steel platter and a cushion in the company's signature shade of green, both shaped to look like the controller's sunken cross-shaped D-pad.

Clever storage is another theme that runs through the collection, often set on casters or equipped with handles so it can easily be moved around the home and turn any room into a game station.

Read:

IKEA unveils inflatable chair that "challenges traditional gaming design"

Most notably, there's IKEA's first go at creating a TV stand since a failed attempt in 2012.

Set on casters, it can be rolled wherever it is needed, while opting for a square over a tubular metal frame keeps it from looking too much like office furniture, explained IKEA designer Lukas Bazle.

"Our focus here was to make a TV stand that's really safe, sturdy and affordable, and that looks good in a lot of different homes," he said.

"Doing a product like that at IKEA is sometimes harder than you'd think. We test our furniture very intensely, and with a TV and castors involved, a lot of things can go wrong."

There's also a wooden toolbox for holding various gaming gear and paraphernalia, which doubles as a laptop stand, as well as a rolling side table with integrated charging stations and a lounge chair with hidden storage pockets below the seat.

Its bouncy, cantilevered design was conceived to support both active and leisurely play.

"I hadn't thought at all about people playing in different modes," Bazle said.

"You sit forward when the game needs your full attention, and then there are games you play to relax, where you're sunk into the chair, and it's a completely different way of sitting. The lounge chair had to handle both."

The pieces are rendered in timber and muted neutrals of black, white and grey, with splashes of green guiding the eye to the integrated storage.

IKEA has gone full-force on gaming furniture in recent years, with previous launches including an inflatable gaming chair and a range of high-tech desks and chairs with Republic of Gamers.

item.content:encoded:
Developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics have designed three flats based on what a 25-year-old can afford to buy in Sweden today, with the smallest micro home measuring just 1.9 square metres.

The sizes of the three apartments were based on Riksbyggen's square metre index, which calculates how many square metres of housing a young person can afford based on income, property prices and mortgage conditions.

The calculations were made using data from government agency Statistics Sweden (SCB) and digital bank Avanza.

Riksbyggen and BBDO Nordics looked at incomes in three Swedish cities – Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå – to create a broad geographical spread when calculating the size of the homes, which the companies are calling Sweden's smallest apartments.

"Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå are among the Swedish cities where young people have a particularly strong need for housing, while also facing significant difficulties finding and affording it," BBDO Nordics art director Anton Bolin told Dezeen.

"Together, the three cities show that the issue affects young people across Sweden, from south to north."

After calculating what a 25-year-old with the national average income and savings could afford to buy in each city, the companies designed three tiny apartments: one measuring 1.9 square metres for Stockholm, a 3.1-square-metre flat for Gothenburg and a 4.5-square-metre home for Umeå.

"The idea is to make the housing crisis facing young people visible and tangible," Bolin said. "We see numbers and statistics about it everywhere, but they can easily become abstract."

"So we wanted to show exactly how much home an average 25-year-old can afford today, and let people experience that reality."

Bolin then worked with Bengt Svedlund from Stockholm company Dekormakarna to create the three flats, which were designed to look typically Swedish.

"We wanted the houses to look like typical Swedish homes, the kind of houses you see all over the country," Bolin said. "With familiar architecture and details, but at an unusual scale that makes the absurdity of the situation immediately clear."

Each of the three buildings has a distinctive design, ranging from more classical building types to contemporary housing.

"The first is inspired by turn-of-the-century style, with a rendered facade in 'Stockholm yellow', herringbone flooring, mullioned windows and ceiling mouldings," Bolin explained.

Read:

Eight innovative micro homes that make small sites feel big

"The second draws on 1930s/40s functionalism, with clean lines, light pastel colours, linoleum flooring and a corrugated metal balcony," he continued.

"The third represents contemporary housing, with a brick facade and simpler, more functional materials."

One in five young people in Sweden still live with their parents, according to Bolin, who hopes that the project will ultimately help to rally public support for more affordable housing.

"We hope the project gets more people talking about the problem and puts housing higher on the political agenda," he said.

"That's why we launched the project ahead of Sweden's general election in September 2026. Our hope is that the next government will take action on the three housing reforms we believe are needed."

Previous micro homes featured on Dezeen include a house in a former wind turbine and an "aspirational" housing prototype in India.

The photography is by Jörgen Brennicke from Rockson.
